transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-21
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Recorders: Fireflies.ai
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Jordan Kim (Redwood CSM), Tom Nguyen (CTO, AtlasPay), Maya Lopez (Eng Manager, AtlasPay), Diego Rivera (SRE, AtlasPay)

Summary (auto): POC scoping to choose deployment mode. Discussed success criteria (latency targets, cost envelope, eval pass rates), workload sizing, benchmark methodology, and timelines for a 4-week POC. Security and data residency noted as gating factors for Private deployment.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Samir: hey everybody, thanks for joining, we uh, we really appreciate you taking the time. quick intros?
[00:00:10] Tom: hey, tom here, cto at atlaspay. maya and diego are with me.
[00:00:15] Maya: morning — eng manager, owning integrations and infra for ml features
[00:00:20] Samir: awesome, i'm samir — account exec at redwood, and lena is our solutions engineer, she'll run through the benchmark plan and sizing. jordan from cs will help with onboarding and billing questions.
[00:00:35] Lena: hi everyone, quick agenda: success criteria, traffic profile, benchmark tests (latency/throughput/quality), and then timelines — feel free to interrupt.
[00:00:48] Diego: sounds good. we have a couple constraints: PCI environment, some PII, and we need to keep logs in us-east only for now.
[00:00:58] Samir: noted — data residency and PCI are common asks; we'll cover private options and dedicated with VPC.
[00:01:12] Tom: high level — use case is contextual payment assistance inside our merchant dashboard, about 2M queries/month estimated after ramp, bursty traffic around merchant peak times. latency matters for UX, target p95 under 200ms ideally. cost is also important — we have a rough budget for inference of $X per month (we'll share exact).
[00:01:35] Maya: and quality metrics: we have an eval set of ~500 prompts that represent QA/regression checks; we want parity or improvement vs our current self-hosted model.
[00:01:50] Lena: perfect — so typical success criteria we see: p95 latency target, pass rate on eval set (like >=95% of current baseline), and cost per 1M tokens below a threshold. are those aligned?
[00:02:05] Tom: yes. also uptime and ability to route to a cheaper fallback model during peak if needed.
[00:02:13] Samir: great. quick clarification on deployment modes: Hosted = fastest onboarding, we run in our hosted infra with encryption at rest and options for retention; Dedicated = reserved GPU pool for you in our infra, better isolation and predictable throughput; Private = bring-their-own VPC or on-prem package, needed for strict compliance.
[00:02:40] Tom: how different are the p95 numbers between hosted and dedicated?
[00:02:45] Lena: in our benchmarks for similar workloads, hosted p95 for short context (up to 512 tokens) typically around 80–160ms depending on model and region; dedicated can reduce variance and tail latency, often tightening p95 by 10–30% if we dedicate capacity and optimize batching. but cost patterns change — dedicated has commit cost but lower unit price at scale.
[00:03:10] Maya: what's the throughput limits for dedicated? we need to handle bursts to ~500 rps for short internal calls during peak.
[00:03:20] Lena: ok, 500 rps short-lived bursts is feasible with dedicated pools and autoscale policies plus burst capacity; we'll size GPU count and batchers accordingly. for hosted, we can often handle bursts but you don't get guaranteed capacity — we recommend a test to see real-world behavior.
[00:03:40] Diego: and what about private — we have corporate policy that suggests private for anything touching payment credentials even if we tokenize, because of auditors. is private on-prem supported?
[00:03:52] Samir: yes, we offer private deployments — cloud VPC-private control plane and an on-prem package for air-gapped. that path requires more lead time (ops and security reviews) and a different pricing cadence.
[00:04:05] Tom: timeline — how long to run a POC that gives us confidence?
[00:04:12] Lena: practical POC is 3–6 weeks: week 1 onboarding and baseline hosted run, week 2 dedicated sizing and initial benchmarks, week 3 quality evals and iteration, week 4 extension for scale testing and final report. if you want private, add 2–4 weeks for infra work and security signoffs.
[00:04:35] Maya: that aligns. for benchmarks, can you run with our sample traffic (seq length distribution included)? we can provide traces.
[00:04:44] Lena: yes — best is you share traffic profile: qps vs hour, seq length histogram, top prompt families. we'll run latency p50/p95/p99, throughput (tokens/sec), cost estimates and quality eval on your eval set.
[00:05:00] Tom: about quality, are you able to run our eval set in both hosted and dedicated and show differences? we suspect quantization or different kernels might change output.
[00:05:10] Lena: absolutely — we'll run the same prompts across deployments and record logits, outputs, and automated metrics plus a handful of manual spot checks. quantization differences can change behavior; we'll flag any regressions.
[00:05:22] Diego: security specifics — we need SOC 2 type II, SSO via SAML, audit logs for all model calls, and KMS integration for key management. can you support that?
[00:05:33] Samir: yes — we support SAML SSO, audit logs, and KMS/HSM integrations. for SOC 2 docs we can share our report and a security pack. for private on-prem we'll map to your existing KMS/tenant keys.
[00:05:48] Maya: do you have any benchmarks around cost per 1M tokens for the models we discussed?
[00:05:54] Lena: ballpark depends on model and quantization; for mid-sized open models on dedicated you may see unit costs 30–50% lower than fully hosted at high commit, but it's very workload dependent — the benchmark spreadsheet we'll send has a cost model to plug in your ratio of generations vs embeddings and avg tokens per call.
[00:06:10] Tom: ok — for our POC success criteria: 1) p95 < 200ms for our core flows, 2) quality parity with our baseline (>=95% on eval pass rate), 3) cost <= their internal target (we'll send exact number), and 4) demonstration of routing/fallback and observability in the console.
[00:06:27] Samir: perfect — i'll capture those as the scoping success criteria.
[00:06:33] Lena: technical note: for latency-sensitive flows we recommend using KV cache and prefix caching. also tune batching windows to balance p95 vs throughput. we'll propose batching configs in the plan.
[00:06:46] Maya: curious about autoscaling — will dedicated autoscale automatically or do we need to set policies?
[00:06:52] Lena: you configure autoscale policies; we can suggest defaults (target CPU/GPU util thresholds, warm-up rules). Dedicated supports burst capacity for short windows to avoid cold drop.
[00:07:05] Diego: do you record inputs? our policy is to not persist raw PII — we need to know where and for how long logs exist.
[00:07:14] Samir: we have configurable retention; hosted defaults to X days but can be shortened. redwood has options to disable input retention for sensitive tenants. private obviously gives you full control. we'll include that in security doc.
[00:07:28] Tom: ok next, benchmarks — what exact tests will you run?
[00:07:32] Lena: plan: synthetic latency tests (single-request latency across seq lengths), throughput sweep (increase qps until p99 or error), and real-eval run (run your 500 prompts and compute pass rate and diff). we'll also run a mixed workload simulating burst patterns from your traces.
[00:07:55] Maya: can we see raw logs and traces in the console? instrumentation for token-level cost breakdown is critical for our finance team.
[00:08:03] Jordan: yes, console exposes token-level cost, per-route model breakdowns, and tracing hooks — we can provide a demo.
[00:08:10] Samir: action items: i'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and sample pricing; lena will draft sizing for dedicated; maya to share traffic profile.
[00:08:21] Tom: perfect. one more question — if during peak we need guaranteed throughput, is dedicated the only option?
[00:08:29] Lena: dedicated gives guarantees. hosted can be supplemented with rate-limiting and fallback to smaller models but it's not capacity-guaranteed. for strict SLOs we recommend dedicated or private with reserved capacity.
[00:08:44] Diego: what about failover across regions? we need active-active for DR.
[00:08:49] Samir: we support multi-region routing; for hosted we can route to nearest region, for dedicated you'd need reserved capacity in both regions or rely on cross-region fallbacks. private will need your infra configured for multi-region.
[00:09:05] Maya: anything else we should be aware of technically?
[00:09:08] Lena: model quantization choices, sequence length distribution, and prompt engineering will all affect latency/cost. we'll flag chokepoints after initial runs.
[00:09:18] Tom: ok let's wrap with timeline recap.
[00:09:22] Samir: tentative timeline: 10/22 — we share plan, 10/23 — AtlasPay provides traffic and SLO doc, week of 10/27 — hosted baseline run, week of 11/03 — dedicated pilot and scale tests, 11/10 — final report and recommendation. if private is chosen, add 2–4 weeks for infra.
[00:09:44] Maya: that works for us, we'll try to get traffic profile by 10/23.
[00:09:48] Tom: we'll also share the exact cost target and compliance checklist.
[00:09:52] Samir: great — thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the benchmark spreadsheet and security pack.
[00:09:58] Jordan: i'll set up a calendar invite for the hosted baseline and include the onboarding docs.
[00:10:05] Tom: thanks all.
[00:10:07] Maya: thanks.
[00:10:10] [call ended]

Notes about transcription: occasional mis-attributions and filler words preserved. Some product names and acronyms might be slightly off (e.g., kv-cache spelled out as KV cache).
